claims.text: A V-Cr-Ti-W refractory high-entropy alloy can be used in plasma-facing components.
V, Cr, Ti, and W constitute a low-activation elemental design.
Under fusion-relevant conditions, the V-Cr-Ti-W alloy will have better mechanical integrity than conventional tungsten materials or reduced-activation steels.
Under fusion-relevant conditions, the V-Cr-Ti-W alloy will have greater irradiation resistance than conventional tungsten materials or reduced-activation steels.
The V-Cr-Ti-W alloy will produce lower long-term residual radioactivity than conventional tungsten materials or reduced-activation steels.
Arc melting followed by homogenization produces a V-Cr-Ti-W alloy with a BCC-based multicomponent matrix.
Thermomechanical processing or hot isostatic pressing after melting will refine the alloy microstructure.
Fusion plasma-facing materials must tolerate sustained high-temperature exposure and intense particle and neutron environments.
A temperature of at least 1000 °C represents the relevant exposure condition for the proposed test.
The V-Cr-Ti-W composition stabilizes a refractory high-entropy BCC structure.
The V-Cr-Ti-W compositional design mitigates radiation damage.
High configurational entropy promotes a single-phase or stable dual-phase BCC microstructure in V-Cr-Ti-W.
High configurational entropy causes sluggish diffusion in the V-Cr-Ti-W alloy.
Sluggish diffusion reduces elemental transmutation rates during irradiation.
Sluggish diffusion suppresses irradiation-induced defect growth.
Tungsten is a leading plasma-facing-material candidate but has very low fracture toughness and a restricted operating-temperature window.
The proposed alloy's irradiation tolerance and oxidation resistance above 1200 °C remain unverified.
Additional alloying or protective coatings may be required under extreme temperature and flux conditions.
The quantitative mechanical and activation advantages of the V-Cr-Ti-W alloy have not been established.
